background.definition: Costochondritis is a common, self-limiting clinical syndrome characterized by pain and tenderness in the parasternal joint and/or the upper costochondral junction. It is also called Tietze disease, which is sometimes distinguished from costochondritis by the presence of objective swelling or edema near the affected joints.

list.listitem: Costochondritis was diagnosed in 30% of consecutive patients with chest pain not due to trauma, fever, or malignancy seen in the emergency department.
A study of consecutive episodes of chest pain in primary care practices found that 20% were musculoskeletal in origin.
Costochondritis is more common in women (68%-69% of cases).
The predominant age for patients with costochondritis is older than 40 years; Tietze syndrome is more common in younger patients.
Unknown.
Trauma or viral infection has been suggested.
Inflammation of costal cartilage, perhaps caused by repetitive trauma or viral infection.
Diagnosis is based on the clinical examination; no further diagnostic testing is needed in low-risk young adults without worrisome signs for cardiopulmonary disease. C
Must rule out serious cardiopulmonary causes of anterior chest wall pain in older patients and those with any other cardiopulmonary symptoms. B
Bone scans are not useful. C
Typical patient presents with acute or subacute anterior chest pain.
Pain is worse with chest movement, sneezing, or cough.
Presence of fever, adenopathy, shortness of breath, tachycardia, or other cardiopulmonary symptoms suggest another diagnosis.
Diffuse tenderness is usually seen over one or more costochondral joints.
Swelling over involved costochondral joints occurs in Tietze syndrome.
Routine imaging studies or ECG are not recommended for young patients with typical presentation and no cardiac risk factors or cardiopulmonary symptoms.
Ultrasound may reveal increased echogenicity and a strong, broad, posterior acoustic shadow but is not routinely recommended.
Imaging with bone scans (eg, with 99mTc-methylene diphosphonate) is not useful.

Patients with persistent symptoms, a history of cardiovascular disease or thromboembolism, or other cardiopulmonary symptoms should have further evaluation to rule out bony or cardiopulmonary disease.
Costochondritis is a clinical diagnosis. Rule out cardiopulmonary causes (angina, acute myocardial infarction, and pulmonary embolism) with relevant investigations as needed.
Bone scans not useful. Ultrasound may help to identify significant inflammation or edema but is not routinely recommended.
No relevant H&P rules found.
NSAIDs are useful for pain control and are the mainstay of treatment, but clinical trials are lacking. No specific doses have been published. C

Corticosteroid and/or local anesthetic injections (eg, 15 mg triamcinolone with 1 mL 2% lidocaine) at the specific painful sites have been recommended, but none of these treatments have been tested in a clinical trial. C
The prognosis is good for this self-limited condition. Follow-up is only as needed. C
In 1 case series, more than half of adults diagnosed with costochondritis and Tietze syndrome still had pain 6 months later. C
Costochondritis and Tietze syndrome can recur a number of times. C
